user_text: Explain what a hash table is and when to use it.
assistant_text:
**Hash Table**: Data structure that maps keys to values using a hash function to compute array indices.

**How it works**:
• Hash function converts key → array index
• Store value at that index
• Handle collisions (multiple keys → same index) via chaining or open addressing

**Time complexity**: O(1) average for insert/lookup/delete

**Use when**:
• Need fast key-value lookups
• Implementing caches, databases, sets
• Counting frequencies
• Detecting duplicates

**Avoid when**:
• Need ordered data
• Memory is extremely constrained
• Keys have poor hash distribution

Common implementations: Python dict, Java HashMap, JavaScript Object.

user_text: Summarize the key benefit in one sentence.
assistant_text: Hash tables provide O(1) average-time key-value lookups, making data retrieval nearly instantaneous regardless of dataset size.

user_text: Give one practical example in everyday apps.
assistant_text: **Web browser cache**: Stores webpage data using URLs as keys for instant page loading without re-downloading.

user_text: Name one tradeoff compared to a balanced tree.
assistant_text: **Tradeoff**: Hash tables lose key ordering, while balanced trees maintain sorted data for range queries and ordered iteration.

• **Poor hash function**: Causes clustering/collisions, degrading O(1) to O(n) performance
• **Load factor neglect**: Overfilled table increases collisions; underfilled wastes memory

user_text: State the average time complexity for lookup.
What is a good alternative when memory is tight?
assistant_text: **Sorted array with binary search**: O(log n) lookup but much lower memory overhead than hash tables.
**Library card catalog**: Hash function = filing system that instantly directs you to the right drawer and slot for any book title.

user_text: Describe when I should not use it.
assistant_text:
**Don't use when**:
• Need data in sorted order
• Performing range queries (find all keys between X and Y)
• Memory is severely limited
• Keys hash poorly (many collisions)

user_text: Give one reason it can be faster than a list.
assistant_text: **Direct access**: Hash tables jump straight to the target location, while lists must scan through elements one-by-one.
Hash tables trade memory for speed, delivering instant key-value lookups at the cost of ordering and extra space.

user_text: Answer in a short bullet list.
assistant_text:
• **What**: Key-value storage using hash functions for array indexing
• **Speed**: O(1) average lookup/insert/delete
• **Best for**: Fast lookups, caches, duplicate detection
• **Tradeoff**: Memory overhead, no ordering
• **Avoid when**: Need sorted data or tight memory constraints
